content.content:
**Plans**

| Plan | Fee | Included usage | Key limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free Trial | $0 | $5 one-time credit, expires in 30 days | 2 vCPU / 1 GB per service, 2 replicas |
| Free | $0 | $1/month | 1 vCPU / 0.5 GB per service, 1 replica |
| Hobby | $5/month | $5/month | 48 vCPU / 48 GB per service, 6 replicas |
| Pro | $20/month per workspace | $20/month | 1,000 vCPU / 1 TB per service, 42 replicas, unlimited seats |
| Enterprise | Custom | Custom | Custom, with SLAs and compliance options |

**Usage rates (services, billed per second)**

| Resource | Rate | Approx. per month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory | $0.00000386 per GB/s | $10 per GB |
| CPU | $0.00000772 per vCPU/s | $20 per vCPU |
| Volumes (storage) | $0.00000006 per GB/s | $0.15 per GB |
| Egress | $0.05 per GB | n/a |
| Object storage | $0.015 per GB-month, free egress | n/a |

**Sandboxes (VMs)**

Sandboxes bill on separate rates and draw from the same included credit: about $50 per GB of memory and $50 per vCPU per month while active, plus $0.05 per GB of egress. You pay for CPU actually used and memory held while running, and destroyed sandboxes cost nothing.

**Notes**

- Hobby usage up to $5 in a billing cycle incurs no extra charge. Anything above that is billed. Unused included usage does not roll over.
- Upgrades take effect immediately. Downgrades take effect at the next billing cycle.
- The page does not describe backups, so check https://docs.railway.com/reference/pricing/plans or contact sales for backup details.

content.content:
This page doesn't include the figures you asked for. The instance hourly rates, gp3 storage per-GB prices, and backup storage prices are in collapsed tables whose values aren't in the content provided.

What the page does say:

- **Free tier:** It includes 750 hours on "a selection of Single-AZ instance databases," 20 GB of General Purpose SSD (gp2) storage, and 20 GB of backup storage each month for one year. It doesn't say whether db.t4g.medium is one of the eligible instances.
- **T4g CPU credits:** T4g instances run in Unlimited mode. You're charged $0.075 per vCPU-hour when average CPU use over a rolling 24-hour period exceeds the baseline. This is separate from the instance hourly rate, and Reserved Instances don't cover it.
- **Backup storage:** The page covers automated backups and manual snapshots but gives no per-GB price.
- **Stopped instances:** You're still charged for provisioned and backup storage, but not instance hours.

To get the exact numbers, use the AWS Pricing Calculator (calculator.aws, under RDS for PostgreSQL) with us-east-1, db.t4g.medium, Single-AZ, and gp3. You can also expand the On-Demand section on the RDS pricing page.

Official and secondary sources agree on the core claim, but they differ on PITR eligibility by plan.

- **Retention window:** DigitalOcean's own PostgreSQL page says backups run every day and let you restore data to any point within the previous seven days.
- **Forking to a past point:** A DigitalOcean community answer describes creating a point-in-time copy of a cluster through the fork feature, which creates a copy of your database as of a specific point in time within the last 7 days.
- **Conflict on plan requirements:** A third-party backup vendor (SimpleBackups) says PITR for Postgres is available on Postgres and MySQL higher-tier clusters. Another third-party guide says PostgreSQL and MySQL managed databases support this feature on most plans. Neither is an official DigitalOcean statement, and the official marketing pages I found don't mention tiers, so check the current plan docs before relying on either.
- **Downloads:** The same vendor says You cannot download native backups. I didn't find this confirmed in DigitalOcean's documentation, so treat it as unverified. If you need off-platform copies, a `pg_dump` to external storage is the usual approach.

- **Compute:** Several sources list Launch at $0.106 per CU-hour and Scale at $0.222 per CU-hour (Launch is pay-as-you-go at $0.106 per CU-hour and $0.35 per GB-month. Scale is $0.222 per CU-hour with 1,000 projects and 25 branches.). Scale's higher rate is explained as buying enterprise features rather than faster compute (Scale's higher CU-hour rate buys enterprise features - SOC 2 reports, HIPAA, private networking, a longer restore window - not faster compute.).
- **Storage:** Both paid tiers are listed at $0.35 per GB-month (Storage | 0.5 GB/project | $0.35/GB-month | $0.35/GB-month).
- **Restore window and instant restore:** The Neon pricing page gives a restore window of up to 7 days on Launch and up to 30 days on Scale, with instant restore at $0.20 per GB-month on both (same source, index 2-1). Restore history is billed separately from live storage (It's billed separately from your live database storage at $0.20/GB-month, and grows with the size of your data and how long you retain history.).
- **Base fee (conflicting):** A third-party blog lists Launch at $19/month and Scale at $69/month with 10 GB and 50 GB allowances (index 1-8). Neon's own plans docs instead say for Launch and Scale, the minimum monthly fee is $5. Other sources describe paid plans as pure pay-as-you-go with no plan fee (index 9-2). The official docs are the more reliable reference here, but the blog's $19/$69 figures may be outdated.
- **Egress (conflicting):** The Neon pricing page shows 100 GB included on Launch and Scale, then $0.10/GB (index 2-1). A Prisma comparison and a swyftstack article list 500 GB included (index 5-1 and 9-5).

Neon's pricing page and docs are the best sources. Rates and allowances may have changed, so confirm on neon.com/pricing before relying on any figure.

The search did not turn up a monthly price for a 2 vCPU / 8 GB or 4 GB Performance compute configuration. The official pricing page gives only plan starting prices. The best per-CPU figure comes from a third-party site, and it conflicts with another source.

- **Official plan prices:** The Performance plan starts at $30/month and bills compute hourly. The Performance plan is described as for new applications and internal tools, with hourly billing and zero friction to get started. Its listed limits are up to 8 CPU and 32 GB memory per service.

Next step: check the live configuration and cost calculator on tigerdata.com/pricing, or the docs page on pricing and account management, for the exact 2 vCPU / 8 GB and 4 GB hourly rates. Multiplying the hourly rate by roughly 730 hours gives an approximate monthly cost.

The official Render docs confirm the storage rate and the PITR change, but this search didn't turn up an official monthly price for Basic-4gb or Pro-4gb.

- **Storage rate:** Render's docs say storage is charged at a flat $0.30 per GB per month, prorated to the second, and can be raised in 5 GB steps but never lowered (Storage is billed at a fixed rate of $0.30 per GB per month, prorated to the second.; storage can be increased at any time, to any multiple of 5 GB, and can't be reduced).
- **Pro-4gb price (third-party, unverified):** A Kuberns blog post lists Pro-4GB at about $97/month with 50 GB included, and says storage beyond that costs $0.30 per GB (Pro-4GB | 4 GB | 2 dedicated | 50 GB | ~$97). That page itself says to check render.com/pricing for current figures, so treat it as a rough guide.
- **Basic-4gb:** I found no source for this tier or its price. Render's docs name tiers like Basic-1gb, so Basic-4gb may not exist or may be named differently.
- **PITR:** Official docs say all paid databases receive point-in-time recovery (PITR) automatically. Retention depends on the workspace plan (Your retention period for PITR depends on your workspace's plan), but the 3-day figure in your query isn't confirmed in these results.
- **Professional workspace:** The docs refer to Professional workspaces in the feature-availability section. The Kuberns post instead lists workspace plans as Hobby, Pro, and Scale, so the plan names may have changed. I couldn't confirm which applies.

For exact current prices, PITR retention by workspace plan, and whether Basic-4gb exists, check render.com/pricing and the Postgres docs directly.

Links: [{"title":"backup and restore","url":"https://clickhouse.com/docs/pt-BR/products/managed-postgres/backup-and-restore"},{"title":"postgres on fly by supabase","url":"https://supabase.com/blog/postgres-on-fly-by-supabase.md"},{"title":"backup and restore","url":"https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/backup-and-restore"},{"title":"backup and restore","url":"https://clickhouse.com/docs/cloud/managed-postgres/backup-and-restore"},{"title":"Managed Postgres Backup Recovery Window","url":"https://community.fly.io/t/managed-postgres-backup-recovery-window/25903"},{"title":"postgres on fly by supabase","url":"https://supabase.com/blog/postgres-on-fly-by-supabase"},{"title":"Help needed with managed postgres","url":"https://community.fly.io/t/help-needed-with-managed-postgres/25549"},{"title":"what you should know","url":"https://fly.io/docs/postgres/getting-started/what-you-should-know/"},{"title":"backup and restore","url":"https://clickhouse.com/docs/zh/products/managed-postgres/backup-and-restore"},{"title":"backup and restore","url":"https://clickhouse.com/docs/es/products/managed-postgres/backup-and-restore"}]

I didn't find an official Fly.io Managed Postgres backup page. The closest matches are a Fly community thread and ClickHouse-hosted docs, and they disagree on retention.

- **Fly.io community (staff reply):** A full backup runs daily, with incremental backups roughly hourly. Backups are kept for at least 10 calendar days. A separate user post reports a recovery window of 10 days and asks whether it can be changed. The thread I saw doesn't include an answer on that.
- **ClickHouse docs (Managed Postgres, which may be the same product now):** These describe daily full backups plus WAL archiving every 60 seconds or at 16 MB, which enables point-in-time recovery within the retention window. They list retention as 7 days, with longer retention available on request. The page was last modified July 24, 2026.
- **Fly.io self-managed Postgres (older, not the managed product):** Volume snapshots are kept for 5 days.

The 7-day ClickHouse figure, the 10-day Fly community figure, and the 5-day self-managed figure conflict. I'd treat the Fly community post as the best evidence for Fly's own managed service, but it is informal and may be out of date. Confirm the current retention and point-in-time recovery window with Fly.io support or the official docs before relying on it.
